displayQuote: It isn't what we say or think that defines us, but what we do

meta.title: Who really said "It isn't what we say or think that defines us, but what we do"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not in “Sense and Sensibility”, not anywhere in Austen, and not in the 1995 screenplay either. We searched all three in full.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It isn't what we say or think that defines us, but what we do'?
meta.ogDescription: Austen never wrote it. We searched her complete fiction and the 1995 screenplay; the sentence is in neither.

answer.label: Not Jane Austen — and not the 1995 screenplay either
answer.sourceLine: Quote sites file this under Sense and Sensibility. It is not in that novel, and not in any of the others: a full-text search of Austen’s complete fiction at Project Gutenberg returns no occurrence of “defines us” — or even of the phrase “what we do”. The usual fallback claim, that a screenwriter wrote it, does not survive checking either: the words are absent from Emma Thompson’s published screenplay of the 1995 film ↗ as well. We could not establish who did write it.

source.heading: What the search actually found

docMeta.dd: Not present — six novels, Lady Susan and the juvenilia searched

source.excerpt: It isn’t what we say or think that defines us, but what we do.
trail: Downloaded the Project Gutenberg plain-text editions of all six completed novels plus Lady Susan and Love and Freindship, and searched the combined 4.5 MB of text. “defines us”: 0 matches. “what we do”: 0 matches. As a control, “truth universally acknowledged” returns exactly one. Texts used include Sense and Sensibility ↗ and Pride and Prejudice ↗.

Searched the full text of Emma Thompson’s The Sense and Sensibility Screenplay & Diaries (Newmarket Press, 1995) ↗ — the complete shooting script as published. “defines us”, “what we do”, “what we are” and “fail to do” all return 0 matches. Whatever else this sentence is, it is not a line from that film’s script.

Checked Wikiquote’s Jane Austen page ↗: its Misattributed section carries exactly one entry, and this is not it. Neither the 1995 Sense and Sensibility film page ↗ nor a Wikiquote-wide search for the phrase returns anything.

We are not able to tell you where it came from. A widely repeated account credits Andrew Davies’s 2008 television adaptation with a differently-worded line on the same idea; we could not reach a transcript or any source that documents it, so we are not asserting it. If you can point us at a citable one, tell us ↗.
source.excerptNote: There is no passage to quote here, and that is the finding. Every other page on this site shows you the sentence in its source; this one cannot, because no source for it has been found.

source.rightsNote: No rights status is claimed, because the wording has no established source. Austen’s own writing is long out of copyright and free to use — but this sentence is not Austen’s writing, and whoever composed it may well hold rights in it. Quote it as unattributed, or quote Austen instead.

author.name: Jane Austen
author.heading: About Jane Austen
author.bio: Jane Austen (16 December 1775 – 18 July 1817) published four novels in her lifetime — Sense and Sensibility (1811), Pride and Prejudice (1813), Mansfield Park (1814) and Emma (1815) — all anonymously. Her effects are built out of paragraphs rather than epigrams, which is exactly why so much of what circulates as “Jane Austen” turns out to have been written for a camera by somebody else.

copyAttribution: Jane Austen did not write “It isn’t what we say or think that defines us, but what we do.” It appears nowhere in her complete fiction, and nowhere in Emma Thompson’s published 1995 Sense and Sensibility screenplay either. Its real origin is undetermined. Via quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Two claims travel with this sentence. Both are checkable, and both fail.

items.why: A full-text search of the Project Gutenberg edition ↗ returns no match for “defines us”. Nor does any other Austen text.
Often offered as the real source. The published screenplay ↗ does not contain the phrase in any form.

misattribution.truthLine: The safe statement is the negative one: this is not a sentence Jane Austen wrote. For the positive half, see Wikiquote’s sourced Austen page ↗ for lines that genuinely are hers.

context.heading: Why so many “Austen quotes” are not Austen
lead: Austen is funny in paragraphs, not in slogans. Her irony depends on the sentence before it and the one after, which makes her very hard to excerpt and very easy to improve upon — and improving upon her is exactly what adapters are paid to do.
The result is a large body of Austen-flavoured aphorism that has never been inside an Austen novel. Some of it is traceable to a specific screenwriter. This one is not yet traceable to anybody.
context.pull: We can prove where it is not from. That is still an answer.
